The question this page answers

Is digital finance becoming durable financial use — or do the available data still mainly measure infrastructure and transactions?

Payments: more reported terminals, use not measured

Point-of-sale (POS) terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden rose from 561 to 1,651 between March 2025 and June 2026, within its reporting scope; how many people use them is not measured. Administrative payment data can show devices, accounts, transactions and values at high frequency. They are useful signals about the payment system, but each counts a different object, and none can be turned into a number of people or an inclusion outcome without a documented method.

What this does not establish

What payment growth does not establish

More terminals do not prove more unique users. More transactions do not reveal how many people used the service. Nominal transaction value does not show real purchasing-power growth. Accounts, wallet subscribers and registrations are not necessarily active people. A rule, project or new institution is not observed adoption. And successful cash delivery or opening an account is not proof of durable post-transfer use. The payment-system figures here are reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden; this evidence base holds no payment-system statistics from the Central Bank of Yemen – Sana'a.

What we still do not know

What is still missing to measure use

This resource still lacks a comparable, privacy-safe measure of unique and repeat payment users across providers and payment systems, with frequency, recency, transaction purpose, failed/abandoned attempts and clear active-use definitions. It also lacks the downstream usage series needed to measure adoption after major payment-system milestones. The FMIIP results framework itself keeps operational state, participating institutions, use cases, merchant acceptance, active accounts, customer transaction costs and electronic-payment beneficiaries as separate measures; project targets remain targets until they are observed.

03Analysis

POS: three different signals

Within the reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), reported POS terminals rose from 561 to 1,651 between March 2025 and June 2026, transaction counts from 8,015 to 27,504 (after a high of 36,201 in May 2026) and nominal transaction value from YER 320 million to YER 1,045 million (after a high of YER 1,579 million in May 2026). This page keeps these three measures separate. A terminal is infrastructure, a transaction is an event and transaction value is a nominal monetary amount; none equals a person. The transaction series supports only a narrower reading: the totals CBY-Aden reports are higher in June 2026 than in March 2025, but they did not rise steadily and fell in several months; whether the reporting scope stayed the same, including across the change of release format in July 2025, has not been verified.

04What it means

Before comparing payment numbers, ask what each one counts

Cards, accounts, e-wallet subscribers, POS terminals and transactions count different things. Accounts or subscribers may contain duplication or inactivity; terminals are infrastructure; transactions are events. A people-level inclusion rate requires a documented unique-person method rather than a division of administrative totals by population.

Another view of the evidence
05Evidence

E-wallet subscribers: figures from two reports that do not form one series

The CBY-Aden payments report for the third quarter of 2024 gives e-wallet subscriber counts of 414,631 for Q1, 507,585 for Q2 and 581,075 for Q3. The first-half 2025 infographic reports 2,102,484 subscribers. The two publications' subscriber definitions and reporting scope have not been reconciled, so the 2025 figure is not joined to the 2024 quarters and the difference is not read as growth. A subscriber count is not a count of unique people or of active users, and neither publication measures how many adults use a wallet.

Why the numbers differ: the January 2025 baseline of the World Bank-financed FMIIP project counts 375,252 active e-wallet accounts (record FMIIP-BASELINE-2025-01), far fewer than the 2,102,484 subscribers CBY-Aden reports for the first half of 2025. The project defines an active e-wallet account as one used for at least one financial transaction in the last 90 days; the CBY-Aden payments infographic for the first half of 2025 gives no definition of a subscriber. The two have not been reconciled, so the gap cannot be read as growth, as inactivity or as an error, and neither is a count of people. Likewise, CBY-Aden reports 5,202,019 accounts for the first half of 2025, while the project counts 1,062,441 active bank accounts in January 2025 — current accounts with at least one transaction in a year. The two differ in unit, universe and date, and no ratio between them is published or implied.

06System context

What FPS and RTGS mean — and what they do not yet prove

The World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) separates three payment-infrastructure jobs. The Fast Payment System (FPS) is the project’s fast electronic-payment component, which the project supports in areas under the internationally recognized government. The Real-Time Gross Settlement system (RTGS), to be managed by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) alongside an upgrade of its core banking system, is the settlement backbone the project links to large-value payments between financial institutions. A third component supports access and use through access-point mapping, capacity building for financial institutions and payment service providers, merchant onboarding in underserved areas and outreach. Separately, CBY-Aden records from 2026 show a board decision on what the source calls a national QR standard and e-wallet interconnection, unified-network integration work, and the establishment and governance of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company (YPCC). These records show what architecture and institutions are being built; they do not by themselves establish go-live, reliability, transaction coverage, active use or inclusion outcomes. The project's appraisal document (May 2025) adds a design rule: only registered clients of regulated financial institutions may use FPS, and walk-in and over-the-counter transactions, in which the sender or the recipient holds no account at a regulated financial institution, are excluded until a National Risk Assessment is completed and risk-mitigation measures are adopted. That is a design condition, which would leave people without an account outside the system, not evidence that the system operates.

07Analysis

Historical e-money evidence shows why registration cannot be read as durable use

Within a study of five e-money providers by the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS), e-money accounts reached 807,919 in December 2019, while the same source reports an average 23% dormant/inactive share and notes that some accounts were used once or because circumstances imposed their use. CauseWay’s reproducible grouping of the source’s 2019 transaction-value table indicates 57.03% cash-in/cash-out, 29.97% movement between bank and electronic accounts, and 2.41% for bills and purchases together. These are historical patterns within the study’s providers, not current national prevalence.

Why the numbers differ: the 807,919 e-money accounts of December 2019 and CBY-Aden's 414,631 to 581,075 e-wallet subscribers in the first three quarters of 2024 (record CLM-010) cannot be read as a fall. The first counts accounts at the five providers one study of the Institute of Banking Studies (IBS) covered; the second counts subscribers under CBY-Aden's own definition and reporting scope. The two have not been reconciled, and neither counts people.

More evidence and context

More detail on this question, each item with its own period and limits.
Evidence

June 2026 was the latest monthly POS release on CBY-Aden's Arabic payments page as checked on 3 October 2026; its English payments page still ends at January 2026

The Arabic payments page of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 3 October 2026, publishes monthly POS releases from March 2025 through June 2026; the English payments page, checked the same day, still ends at January 2026. This resource therefore stops the monthly series at June 2026. That does not mean activity stopped; it means no later monthly release had been published on the Arabic page when it was checked.

A rule can be issued, infrastructure can expand, institutions can be created and transactions can appear while evidence on reach, repeated use, service quality, protection and outcomes remains incomplete.

What measurement would change the decision?

Measurement priorityP0 · Payments / People
Active and repeat digital use
Evidence needed: Administrative data from providers or payment systems, with deduplication rules, and/or demand-side active-use measures.
Open this measurement priority
Measurement priorityP1 · Identity / Digital access
Digital onboarding and identity journeys
Evidence needed: Journey-level administrative or survey data across onboarding stages: identity and KYC verification, attempts, completion, rejection, abandonment, time and cost.
Open this measurement priority
Measurement priorityP0 · Social protection / Payments
Persistence of financial use after cash transfers
Evidence needed: Longitudinal programme or provider cohort data, or repeated beneficiary follow-up, with privacy-safe linkage from transfer receipt to account or wallet activation, repeat use, merchant use, saving and cash-out.
Open this measurement priority
Measurement priorityP0 · Reforms / Payments / Quality
Reform transmission and service quality
Evidence needed: Reform-specific operational and user-side evidence tied to the same implementation timeline, from go-live through coverage, reliability, cost and outcome.
